title: First-touch Chemistry Kit — SDK starter experiments & failure hypotheses
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, experimental starter kit idea for first-touch SDK onboarding — we call it the "Chemistry Kit" because the goal is to let a developer mix a tiny set of components (sample app, local emulator, a tiny prompt set, a telemetry probe) and immediately see the effects.

Audience:
- New product engineers trying Redwood API for the first time
- Platform/integrator engineers evaluating embedding/streaming behavior
- Solutions engineers running short POC days with customers

Non-goal: full polished docs. This is intentionally small, opinionated, and observable-first.

Top-level hypothesis:
If we give engineers a 10–15 minute tangible loop (code -> run -> observe token and latency metrics -> tweak batching/quant) they will hit "aha" faster and convert to a self-serve flow.

Minimum components in the kit (v0):
- Tiny sample app (Node + Python variants) that calls Redwood API with 3 routes: quick-generate, chat-stream, embedding-bulk.
- Local stub runtime (hermetic devserver) that simulates latency and adds optional failure injection.
- Telemetry probe: a minimal dashboard (static HTML) that shows per-request token count, latency, model variant, and a rolling quality score from a tiny eval prompt set.
- Quick checklist README with 6 steps and a one-paragraph explanation of each toggle (batch size, quantize flag, prefix cache).

Experiment recipes (10–15 min flows):
1) Latency-aware toggle: change batching from 1 -> 8, observe latency percentile and tokens/unit cost in the probe. Record: p50, p95, token count.
2) Fallback resilience: flip a mock zone outage, observe automatic fallback to regional variant and a 503->200 fallback flow.
3) Quality regression gate: enable a new quantized model variant and run the 10-sample eval set; see quality delta in probe and a pass/fail marker.

Failure hypotheses we want to validate quickly:
- New users assume batching always reduces latency — we should catch the cases where batching increases p95 for short-chat flows.
- Telemetry is invisible: if the first loop doesn't show cost/latency, developers ignore optimization knobs.
- Fallback behavior surprises integrators (they don't trust silent model swaps).

Observability and metrics (what the kit surfaces):
- Per-request: route, seq_len, tokens_in, tokens_out, model_tag, quant_flag, batch_size, latency_ms.
- Derived: cost_estimate_usd, p50/p95, quality_score (0..1 based on golden prompts).
- Traces: request id -> whether fallback triggered, which variant handled the request.

Sample README quick steps (to be copy/pasted in the kit):
1) clone repo && npm i or pip install -r requirements.txt
2) set REDWOOD_KEY=demo_local && ./devserver --latency=75 --fail-rate=0.05
3) open ./probe/index.html and run the "quick-generate" route (POST /generate)
4) toggle batch_size in config and re-run; watch p95 in the probe
5) try "simulate-region-failure" in devserver and confirm fallback-to-variant in probe
6) run ./scripts/run-eval.sh to compare model variants and see pass/fail gating

Voice/UX notes (developer experience):
- Use conversational, second-person language: "Try toggling batch size", not "Change the config".
- Show the cost impact visually (graph + dollar estimate) — people respond quickly to $ numbers.
- Keep sample prompts short and domain-neutral but include one long-turn prompt to reveal KV cache behavior.

Safety and security reminders:
- Local devserver should default to non-networked mode.
- Example keys must be obvious fakes; include a script to scrub any real key from sample config.

Integration hooks for adoption funnel:
- When user runs eval with a failing quality gate, prompt a short recommended action: rollback to model x, try quant flag off, or file a ticket with stack trace (automated template).
- Provide a one-click snippet to open a support ticket prefilled with telemetry (id, p95, token counts, model_tag).

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- Do we bundle the local devserver binary (easier UX) or require a container build? (Trade: size vs friction)
- How opinionated should default knobs be? (Conservative defaults reduce surprise but hide capability)
- Do we include a tiny SaaS-hosted probe for users who skip the local HTML step? (Benefits: better telemetry; Cost: infra/support)

Acceptance criteria for shipping a v0 kit:
- Developer can complete at least one experiment recipe in under 15 minutes on mac/linux.
- Probe shows per-request cost and p95 correctly for both language and embed routes.
- At least two internal SEs can reproduce and give >70% usability score in quick feedback survey.

Next steps (short-term backlog):
- [ ] Prototype devserver with latency/failure flags (owner: Omar) — target 2 weeks.
- [ ] Draft README and 6-step checklist (owner: Maya) — 3 days.
- [ ] Build probe simple HTML + JS with sample graphs (owner: Leah) — 1 week.
- [ ] Hook run-eval.sh to emit JSON report for one-click ticketing (owner: Jonas) — 2 weeks.

Notes-to-self / scratch ideas:
- Embed a "compare two routes" diff view that overlays p95 curves (use small sparklines).
- Include a tiny gamified hint system: "Did you try turning batching to 1?"
- Consider making a "deceptively simple" mobile demo to hand to product folk during sales calls.

If you have minutes: please drop quick reactions in #devexp or add comments to the Linear ticket DEVEXP-311.
